% APPENDIX A.5: MERGE VARIANTS COMPARED
% Added 2026-09-17 at the user's request. Appendix A carries TIES and DARE among eight arms; this
% appendix isolates the merge variants against the untuned model, so the only thing varying between
% columns is the sparsification step. That isolation is what makes the Granite result legible.
%
% Tables generated by scripts/analysis/59_master_tables.py into tables/merge_variants_*.tex and
% refreshed in place here by scripts/paper/inline_tables.py via the >>> GENERATED TABLE markers.
\section{Ablation of the Sparsification Step}
\label{app:mergevariants}

Appendix~\ref{app:absmaster} reports \textsc{TIES} and \textsc{DARE-TIES} among eight arms. This
appendix ablates one decision inside our method. The columns hold everything fixed except the
sparsification step of Section~\ref{sec:merging}: magnitude
top-$k$ for \textsc{TIES} (Eq.~\ref{eq:trim}), a random drop with rescaling for \textsc{DARE-TIES}
(Eq.~\ref{eq:dare}), and that same drop without the sign election of Eq.~\ref{eq:elect} for
\textsc{DARE-linear}. Everything else --- the six ingredient specialists, the uniform weights, the
density $0.5$, and the \texttt{total} majority-sign rule --- is held fixed.

The comparison matters for one model in particular. On Granite-3.1-8B
(Table~\ref{tab:merge_variants_granite318b}) \textsc{DARE-TIES} is the only merge in the study that
falls below the untuned model on the backward task, while \textsc{TIES} on the same specialists is
well above it. Read against the other seven models, where the two variants agree, this localises the
failure to \textsc{DARE}'s random drop rather than to sign-consensus merging, It does not change the method --- \textsc{DARE-TIES} is what we use and report throughout --- but it
bounds where that method is reliable, and it identifies the random drop as the component to revisit
if a deployment resembles Granite.
